Usman: Sure thing. Sounds like a heavy workload for those hands. What were you thinking of getting?

Jolie: I was planning on just regular polish. My thought is if I just slap on a fresh coat of topcoat every day or two, it’ll seal everything up and last just as well as gel, but easier to take off.

Usman: I get the appeal of easy removal, but honestly, topcoat doesn't bond to chipped edges. Once water gets under there during your chores, the whole layer lifts. You'll be picking at flakes by Tuesday.

Usman: Just come clean. No lotion or oil. Oil ruins the bond. Speaking of oil, crows are known to drop hard shells on roads so cars crack them open. They understand cause and effect and use traffic as a tool. Smart guys.

Benicio: Look, I get the math, seriously. But kites breathe. That brace line holds everything up. You glue stuff to the spine, you change how the whole frame flexes. It’ll flutter like a leaf and probably crash into the rocks. Trust me on this one.

She is polite but eager to get the correct answer quickly, viewing Victor’s chattiness as a potential delay to her engineering solution. She wants to prove her logic is sound.

Victor, on the other hand, wants to guide Selah toward a solution that actually works without crushing her confidence. He enjoys teaching and sharing his knowledge, but he dislikes watching people waste money on misunderstood concepts. He wants to gently correct her misconception about how wood moves relative to box joints, ensuring she builds something that will last. He is not trying to be a lecturer; he is trying to be a helpful neighbor who happens to know how wood behaves. He values the relationship and the craft, preferring a casual, friendly exchange over a formal critique. He plans to let her state her case, then pivot to the real issue—the width of the opening—while keeping the mood light and encouraging. Selah: Hey Victor, do you have a sec? I’m looking at this quartersawn oak for the lid of this keepsake box, and I need a sanity check on the mechanics before I cut it.

Victor: I see what you’re getting at. It’s a smart thought, honestly. But here’s the thing, Selah. Wood doesn’t really move much along the length. The lid sliding back and forth? That’s lengthwise. That’s the one direction that barely changes. The real enemy is the width of the box opening itself. If the sides swell, the hole gets smaller, and the lid gets stuck. The lid’s grain orientation doesn’t really save you from the box walls tightening up.

Selah: Wait, so the quartersawn lid doesn’t help? That’s the whole point. If the lid stays the same width, it shouldn’t bind. The box walls are flat-sawn, sure, but if the lid is stable, there’s clearance. I’m not sure I follow why the lid’s stability doesn’t matter if the opening shrinks.

Victor: It’s not that the lid’s stability doesn’t matter at all, but it’s not the main lever you’ve got. Think about it. If the box walls swell half a millimeter, the opening shrinks a full millimeter. A quartersawn lid might not change size, but it’s still stuck in a smaller hole. You’re fighting the box, not the lid. You’d be better off focusing on how you join the box sides, or maybe using a liner material that’s less reactive to humidity, rather than just buying more expensive oak for the top.

Victor: You could use a thin strip of something stable for the runners, like maple or even plastic tape, glued to the underside of the lid. That gives you a low-friction surface that doesn’t swell. Or, you can build the box slightly oversized and accept a tiny bit of play. It’s a trade-off. Perfect fit in summer means no fit in winter. You gotta pick your poison.

Selah: Runners sound cleaner. I like that. Do you have any maple scraps I can use, or do I need to source that separately? I want to keep the look consistent.

Victor: I’ve got a scrap bin over in the corner. Probably some maple scraps in there from that cabinet job last month. Let me go check. Give me a second. I’ll grab a few pieces that look straight.

Selah: Thanks. I’ll start measuring the groove width so we know exactly how thick the runners need to be. I want them to slide flush with the bottom.

Victor: That’s the spirit. Nice and flush. Look, if you need a hand clamping those runners in while the glue sets, I’m around. It’s a fiddly job, but you’ve got a steady hand.

Selah: I appreciate that. I’ll probably just use small clamps and weight it down. It’s a small box, so the pressure should be even. I’ll head over to the scrap bin when you get back.

Victor: Sounds like a plan. I’ll see what I can dig up. Don’t rush, take your time measuring. Good wood waits for good hands.
